How Much Is a 5% Raise? The $2,410.50-a-Year Answer, Worked Out Line by Line

Direct AnswerA 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 gross — you keep $2,410.50 after federal tax and FICA. Salary ladder, per-paycheck math and inflation test, worked out.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 6, 2026•12 min read•Calculation Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: $3,000 Gross, $2,410.50 KeptWhat a 5% Raise Actually MeansThe Salary Ladder: What 5% Is Worth at Every Pay LevelPer Paycheck: What the Raise Looks Like Every Two WeeksIf You Are Paid Hourly: $25 to $26.25 an HourThe Bracket Myth: Does a Raise Push You Into a Higher Bracket?Does a 5% Raise Beat Inflation?The Compounding Raise: 5% Every Year for Five YearsRaise vs One-Time Bonus: Same Year One, Different Year FiveAsking for 7% Instead of 5%: What the Ask Is WorthStarting Mid-Year: The July RaiseHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Quick Answer

A 5% raise on a $60,000 salary is $3,000 a year gross — and you keep $2,410.50 of it. Federal income tax takes $360.00, because the whole raise sits inside the 12% bracket, and Social Security plus Medicare take $229.50. That is $92.71 more per biweekly paycheck, $200.88 more a month, and $1.16 more per hour of spending money for every $1.44 of gross raise. About 80 cents of each extra dollar reaches your bank account. The rule behind it is simple — a raise is taxed at your marginal rate, the rate on your last dollar, not your average rate, and only the slice of income above a bracket line ever pays the higher rate.

The Short Answer: $3,000 Gross, $2,410.50 Kept

The question behind this guide is the one people actually type: "how much is a 5% raise?" The answer has two numbers, and the gap between them is the whole point of the guide. The first number is on the letter: 5% of $60,000 is $3,000, and the new salary is $63,000. The second number is on the paycheck: $2,410.50 a year, $92.71 per biweekly check. Here is the whole answer on one worker — $60,000 a year, paid biweekly, single filer in 2026, no state tax — worked out step by step:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross raise5% × $60,000.00$3,000.00
Step 2 — New salary$60,000.00 + $3,000.00$63,000.00
Step 3 — Federal tax on the raise12% × $3,000.00$360.00
Step 4 — FICA on the raise7.65% × $3,000.00$229.50
Step 5 — Take-home value of the raise$3,000.00 − $360.00 − $229.50$2,410.50
Step 6 — Per biweekly paycheck$2,410.50 ÷ 26$92.71

Take-home pay goes from $50,390.00 a year to $52,800.50 a year — the same $50,390.00 our $60,000-after-taxes guide computes, which is the first cross-check on this whole guide. The honesty note: this is a federal-only sketch for a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction. State income tax takes another slice in most states, a 401(k) contribution takes a slice that comes back to you as savings, and health premiums are unchanged by a raise unless the premium itself rises. Our salary increase calculator runs the same gross math at your salary and your percentage, and our paycheck calculator shows the full check with every line.

What a 5% Raise Actually Means

A percentage raise scales with what you already earn: it multiplies your current pay by one plus the percentage. A 5% raise is a multiplier of 1.05, so the new pay is current pay × 1.05 and the raise itself is current pay × 0.05. That scaling is the first thing to understand about a percentage, because the same 5% is a very different amount of money at different salaries — $2,000 on $40,000, $3,000 on $60,000, $5,000 on $100,000 — while a flat-dollar raise of $3,000 is $3,000 whether you earn $40,000 or $100,000. Employers quote percentages precisely because they scale: a 5% raise costs the employer 5% of each person's pay, and it keeps the pay structure in proportion instead of flattening it.

The formula in both directions, with the worked example on the $60,000 anchor:

What you wantFormulaWorked example
Raise amountCurrent pay × raise %$60,000.00 × 0.05 = $3,000.00
New payCurrent pay × (1 + raise %)$60,000.00 × 1.05 = $63,000.00
Raise percentage(New pay − current pay) ÷ current pay × 100($63,000.00 − $60,000.00) ÷ $60,000.00 = 5%
New hourly rateCurrent rate × 1.05$25.00 × 1.05 = $26.25

One mistake shows up everywhere in raise math, and it is worth naming before the rest of the guide: dividing by the new salary instead of the old one. A jump from $60,000 to $63,000 is $3,000 ÷ $60,000 = 5%, not $3,000 ÷ $63,000 = 4.76%. The 4.76% figure answers a different question — what share of the new salary the raise is — and it makes every real raise look smaller than the percentage on the letter. Always divide by what you were earning before. Our hourly-rate guide shows the same divide-by-the-old-number rule for salary-to-hourly conversions, and our gross-versus-net guide explains why the gross figure and the take-home figure are two different numbers in the first place.

The Salary Ladder: What 5% Is Worth at Every Pay Level

The same 5% at five salaries, single filer, 2026 federal brackets (10% to $12,400 of taxable income, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700), standard deduction $16,100, FICA 7.65% on the full raise. Every row is computed the same way — taxable income is gross minus the $16,100 standard deduction, federal tax follows the bracket steps, and the kept column is the raise minus both taxes:

Current salaryNew salaryGross raiseMarginal rateFederal taxFICAYou keepPer biweekly check
$40,000$42,000$2,000.0012%$240.00$153.00$1,607.00$61.81
$50,000$52,500$2,500.0012%$300.00$191.25$2,008.75$77.26
$60,000$63,000$3,000.0012%$360.00$229.50$2,410.50$92.71
$75,000$78,750$3,750.0022%$825.00$286.88$2,638.12$101.47
$100,000$105,000$5,000.0022%$1,100.00$382.50$3,517.50$135.29

Two patterns run through the ladder. First, the kept share falls as the marginal rate rises: at 12% you keep about 80 cents of each extra dollar (12% federal + 7.65% FICA = 19.65% gone), and at 22% you keep about 70 cents (22% + 7.65% = 29.65% gone). The $100,000 row is the proof — $3,517.50 kept on a $5,000 raise is exactly the figure our $100,000-after-taxes guide computes for a $5,000 raise in the same band. Second, the dollar value of the same percentage grows with the salary: the $100,000 worker's 5% is worth $1,107.00 more in take-home than the $60,000 worker's, even though the higher earner keeps a smaller share of each dollar. That is why comparing raises as percentages across people is misleading — a 5% raise for a junior and a 3% raise for a senior can be the same amount of money, and the percentage alone hides it. Our FICA guide explains the 7.65% layer in full, and the 2026 federal tax brackets page shows where each marginal rate starts and stops.

Per Paycheck: What the Raise Looks Like Every Two Weeks

A percentage is abstract; a paycheck is not. Here is the same $60,000 salary with the raises people are most often offered — 3%, 5%, and 10% — converted into the amounts you would actually notice, gross and kept, on the biweekly schedule most US employers use:

RaiseNew salaryGross / yearYou keep / yearGross / biweekly checkKept / biweekly checkKept / month
3%$61,800$1,800.00$1,446.30$69.23$55.63$120.53
5%$63,000$3,000.00$2,410.50$115.38$92.71$200.88
10%$66,000$6,000.00$4,821.00$230.77$185.42$401.75

All three rows sit in the 12% bracket, so every one of them keeps exactly 80.35% of the gross raise — $1,446.30 is 80.35% of $1,800, and $4,821.00 is 80.35% of $6,000. That is the number to carry into a budget: multiply any raise in this band by 0.80 and you are within a few dollars of what actually arrives. Two adjustments change the per-check figure without changing the raise. First, pay frequency: the same $2,410.50 a year is $92.71 on 26 biweekly checks, $100.44 on 24 semi-monthly checks, and $46.36 a week — the annual figure never changes, only the size and timing of the checks. Second, a 401(k) contribution: if you contribute 6% of pay, the contribution takes 6% of the raise too — $180.00 a year on the $3,000 raise — so the kept figure falls to $2,230.50 a year, $85.79 per biweekly check. That $85.79 is worth naming because it matches the top-ranking raise calculator's independently computed figure to the cent, and the difference between $92.71 and $85.79 is not tax at all — it is $6.92 a check going into your own retirement account. Our 401(k) paycheck guide prices that trade in full, and our pay-stub guide shows where the raise first appears on a real stub — usually as a new salary line on the first check of the new pay period, with the year-to-date column catching up a check later.

If You Are Paid Hourly: $25 to $26.25 an Hour

Hourly workers get the same raise, priced per hour instead of per year. A 5% raise on $25.00 an hour is $26.25 an hour — $1.25 more per hour, $2,600.00 more a year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks. The take-home math is the same bracket-step calculation, and it lands on a clean number: federal tax takes $312.00 (12% of $2,600.00), FICA takes $198.90, and you keep $2,089.10 a year — $40.18 a week, or almost exactly $1.00 of spending money for every $1.25 of gross raise. A $1.25-an-hour raise is a $1.00-an-hour raise in your pocket.

The same step at $20.00 an hour: 5% takes the rate to $21.00, $2,080.00 more a year gross, and you keep $1,671.28 of it — $0.80 an hour of spending money for every $1.00 of gross raise. That $1,671.28 is the second cross-check in this guide: it is exactly the difference between our $21-an-hour guide's take-home of $37,276.88 and our $20-an-hour guide's $35,605.60. Two things are different for hourly pay. First, the raise applies to overtime too: at time and a half, the $26.25 rate pays $39.38 an overtime hour where the old $25.00 rate paid $37.50, so an overtime week is worth $1.88 more per overtime hour on top of the straight-time raise. Second, a percentage raise on an hourly rate is the one place where rounding matters — payroll systems round the new rate to the cent, so a 5% raise on an odd rate like $23.47 lands at $24.64, not $24.6435, and the annual figure follows the rounded rate. Run your own rate and hours through our salary increase calculator, which handles hourly wages as well as salaries, and compare the result with our $25-an-hour guide to see the same take-home figure from the other side.

The Bracket Myth: Does a Raise Push You Into a Higher Bracket?

Almost everyone has heard the warning: do not take the raise, it will push you into a higher tax bracket and you will end up with less. The warning is wrong, and the reason is the one fact about brackets that matters most — only the income above a bracket line is taxed at the higher rate. The income below the line keeps its old rate. A raise can never make your take-home pay fall, because the higher rate only ever applies to the slice that crosses the line.

Here is a raise that actually crosses a line, worked out in full. A single filer at $63,500 gets a 5% raise to $66,675 — a $3,175.00 raise. Taxable income moves from $47,400 to $50,575, crossing the $50,400 line where the 22% bracket starts by exactly $175.00:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross raise$66,675.00 − $63,500.00$3,175.00
Step 2 — Taxable income before$63,500.00 − $16,100.00$47,400.00
Step 3 — Federal tax before$1,240.00 + 12% × $35,000.00$5,440.00
Step 4 — Taxable income after$66,675.00 − $16,100.00$50,575.00
Step 5 — Federal tax after$1,240.00 + 12% × $38,000.00 + 22% × $175.00$5,838.50
Step 6 — Federal tax on the raise$5,838.50 − $5,440.00$398.50
Step 7 — FICA on the raise7.65% × $3,175.00$242.89
Step 8 — Take-home value of the raise$3,175.00 − $398.50 − $242.89$2,533.61

The federal tax on the raise is $398.50 — 12.55% of the raise, not 22%. Only $175.00 of the $3,175.00 is taxed at 22%, which costs $38.50; the other $3,000.00 is taxed at 12%, which costs $360.00. If someone applied 22% to the whole raise, the federal tax would come out at $698.50 and the kept figure at $2,233.61 — understating the raise by exactly $300.00, which is the cost of the myth in dollars. The kept figure is $2,533.61 a year, $97.45 per biweekly check. One real edge case does exist, and it is not a bracket: some income-based benefits and credits phase out with income, so a raise can reduce a subsidy or a credit at the same time as it raises pay — but that is a phase-out, not a tax bracket, and it is decided by the benefit's own rules, not by the 22% line. Our paycheck-tax guide walks the same bracket steps on a single check, and the 2026 brackets page lists every line a raise can cross.

Does a 5% Raise Beat Inflation?

A raise is only a raise if it beats the rise in prices. The real raise — the gain in purchasing power — is the nominal raise divided by inflation, minus one: at 3% inflation, a 5% raise is $1.05 ÷ $1.03 − 1 = 1.94% in real terms. On a $60,000 salary, the $63,000 new pay is worth $63,000.00 ÷ 1.03 = $61,165.05 in today's dollars, a genuine $1,165.05 gain. At 5% inflation the same 5% raise is exactly a wash — $1.05 ÷ $1.05 − 1 = 0% — and at 2% inflation it is a 2.94% real raise. The table below prices the same 5% raise at four inflation rates, so the break-even point is visible at a glance:

Inflation rateReal raise$63,000 in today's dollarsReal gain on $60,000Verdict
2%2.94%$61,764.71$1,764.71Clearly ahead
2.8% (2026 COLA pace)2.14%$61,284.05$1,284.05Ahead
3%1.94%$61,165.05$1,165.05Ahead
5%0.00%$60,000.00$0.00A wash

Two benchmarks put the 5% in context. The first is the cost-of-living adjustment: the Social Security COLA for 2026 is 2.8%, so a 2.8% raise on $60,000 — $1,680.00 — is the amount that simply holds your purchasing power still, and a 5% raise beats it by 2.2 percentage points. The second is what other workers are actually getting: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Employment Cost Index shows private-sector wages and salaries up 3.4% over the 12 months ending March 2026, so a 5% raise is 1.6 points ahead of the average worker's year. Both benchmarks say the same thing — 5% is a real raise in 2026, not just a bigger number — but the margin is thin enough that a 3% raise, the bottom of the merit range, would be a real raise of about zero at 3% inflation. If your raise is below the inflation rate, the honest description is a pay cut in real terms, whatever the letter says.

The Compounding Raise: 5% Every Year for Five Years

The most underrated property of a percentage raise is that it repeats. A one-time bonus pays once; a raise becomes the new base, and next year's raise is calculated on top of it. A worker at $60,000 who gets 5% every year for five years does not end up $15,000 ahead — the raises stack, and the fifth year's salary is $76,576.90, not $75,000. Here is the five-year run, with the annual salary each year and the total earned over the five years:

YearSalary at 5% a yearSalary at 3% a year5% lead for the year
Year 1$63,000.00$61,800.00$1,200.00
Year 2$66,150.00$63,654.00$2,496.00
Year 3$69,457.50$65,563.62$3,893.88
Year 4$72,930.38$67,530.53$5,399.85
Year 5$76,576.90$69,556.45$7,020.45
Five-year total$348,114.78$328,104.60$20,010.18

Against a flat $60,000 with no raises at all, five years of 5% raises are worth $48,114.78 of extra gross pay — $348,114.78 earned against $300,000. Against five years of 3% raises, the 5% track is worth $20,010.18 more, and the gap grows every year because the lead compounds: $1,200.00 in year one, $7,020.45 by year five. Stretch it to ten years and the 5% track reaches $97,733.68 a year — the same figure the best compounding tables online show, which is the third cross-check in this guide. The lesson for a review conversation is practical: the percentage you accept this year is the base every future raise is calculated on, so a 2-point difference now is a $20,010.18 difference over five years, not a $1,200.00 difference. That is also why a raise and a bonus are not interchangeable, which is the next section.

Raise vs One-Time Bonus: Same Year One, Different Year Five

Put a $3,000 one-time bonus next to a 5% raise on a $60,000 salary and the first year looks identical. The bonus is $3,000 gross, and its true federal tax at the 12% marginal rate is $360.00, with $229.50 of FICA — a true take-home value of $2,410.50, exactly the same as the raise's first year. The bonus even arrives faster: the raise trickles in at $92.71 a check, while the bonus lands in one payday (minus the 22% supplemental withholding of $660.00, which makes the payday amount $2,110.50 and leaves $300.00 to come back at filing). Year one is a tie. Year two is not.

The bonus pays once and stops. The raise pays $3,000 in year one, $3,150 in year two, $3,307.50 in year three, and keeps growing, because each year's raise is calculated on the higher base. Over five years the raise is worth $48,114.78 of extra gross pay against a flat salary; the one-time bonus is worth $3,000. The gap is $45,114.78 — the price of trading a repeating raise for a single payment. That does not make bonuses bad: a bonus on top of a raise is the best of both, a bonus is real money for a goal this year, and a bonus does not raise the employer's permanent payroll cost the way a raise does, which is exactly why employers offer them. It does make the trade visible. When an employer offers a bonus instead of a raise, price it as one year of the raise, not as the raise itself. Our bonus-tax guide works the same $3,000 bonus through the 22% withholding rule and the refund in full, and our hourly-versus-salary comparison uses the same pricing logic when an offer mixes a salary with a signing bonus.

Asking for 7% Instead of 5%: What the Ask Is Worth

Most raise conversations end with the number on the letter, but the number is negotiable, and the negotiation has a price tag. On a $60,000 salary, the difference between accepting 5% and asking for 7% is 2 points — $1,200.00 a year gross. After 12% federal tax ($144.00) and 7.65% FICA ($91.80), the ask is worth $964.20 a year in take-home pay, $37.08 per biweekly check, $80.35 a month. That is the amount at stake in a single conversation, and it is the amount to weigh against the risk of asking — which, in a normal review, is close to zero, because the worst realistic answer is the original 5%.

The ask compounds, too. If both tracks then get 5% raises each year, the $1,200.00 gap grows: $1,260.00 in year two, $1,323.00 in year three, $1,389.15 in year four, $1,458.61 in year five — $6,630.76 of extra gross pay over five years from one conversation, $5,327.82 of it kept after tax at the 12% band. Three things make the ask easier to win. First, anchor it in the market, not in need: the BLS average is 3.4% and you are asking for 7% on the strength of specific results, not because expenses rose. Second, ask for the percentage and the review date together — a 7% raise now with a six-month check-in is easier to grant than an open-ended promise. Third, know the fallback: if the percentage will not move, ask for the same $1,200.00 as a one-time bonus, a title change, or an earlier review date, and price each fallback against the $964.20 of take-home the percentage was worth. Our salary comparison calculator prices two offers side by side when the negotiation is between employers rather than with your current one, and our $25-an-hour guide shows what the same 5% looks like when the pay is hourly and the ask is per hour.

Starting Mid-Year: The July Raise

Most raises do not start on January 1. They start at a review date, after a promotion, or halfway through the year — and the first year's value is smaller than the headline. A 5% raise on $60,000 that takes effect on July 1 applies to only 13 of the 26 biweekly checks, so the first year's gross gain is $1,500.00, not $3,000.00, and the take-home gain is $1,205.25, not $2,410.50. The second year is the first full year at $63,000, and the raise is worth the full $2,410.50 from then on. The same halving applies to any mid-year start: a raise effective October 1 is worth one quarter of the annual figure in year one, and a raise effective in the last pay period of December is worth almost nothing until January.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the effective date is negotiable and it has a price: moving a 5% raise from July 1 to April 1 on a $60,000 salary is worth three extra months at the new rate — $750.00 gross, $602.63 kept — which is more than half of what asking for an extra point would buy. Second, a mid-year raise does not change the bracket math: the raise is still taxed at your marginal rate on the dollars it adds, and the crossing example in this guide works the same way whether the raise starts in January or July, because the brackets are annual and the raise is annualised on the return. If your employer backdates the raise to the review date, the back pay arrives as a lump sum on one check and is withheld at the same rates — it is the same $1,205.25 spread differently, not extra money.

How to Use the Calculator

Price your own raise in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your current pay and your raise in the salary increase calculator: type your current annual salary (or hourly wage) and either the raise percentage or the new pay — the tool works from either one.
  2. Step 2 — Read the dollar change, not just the percentage: the calculator shows the new pay as an annual, monthly, weekly, and hourly amount, so a 5% raise becomes $3,000 a year, $250.00 a month, $57.69 a week, and $1.44 an hour on a $60,000 salary.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the kept-share rule to the gross figure: at a 12% marginal rate you keep about 80 cents of each extra dollar after federal tax and FICA, and at 22% about 70 cents — the calculator gives you the gross change, and this guide's ladder gives you the take-home.
  4. Step 4 — Test the next number before you ask for it: run 7% through the calculator and read the difference against 5% — $1,200.00 a year gross, $964.20 kept on a $60,000 salary — so you walk into the conversation knowing exactly what the ask is worth.

Limitations

  1. Federal only unless stated: every take-home figure uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction. State and local taxes are excluded, so actual take-home is lower in most states — and the 401(k) and bonus figures name their own assumptions.
  2. One filer, one situation: married filing jointly, head of household, other income, tax credits, and multiple jobs all change the brackets and the kept share. The 80-cent rule holds only while your marginal rate stays at 12%, and the 70-cent rule only at 22%.
  3. Withholding is not your final tax: the per-check figures follow the IRS Publication 15-T percentage method for a single filer. Your return settles the difference, so a bonus withheld at 22% comes back in part at filing, and a raise that crosses a bracket line settles the same way.
  4. Inflation figures are assumptions, not forecasts: the 3% inflation rate and the 2.8% cost-of-living pace are stated benchmarks for the comparison, not predictions. The real-raise table shows the arithmetic at each rate so you can substitute the rate you actually face.
  5. Compounding assumes the raise repeats: the five-year and ten-year figures assume a 5% raise every year. Real raises vary year to year, and a single 5% raise followed by flat years is worth $3,000 a year, not $48,114.78 over five years.
  6. Not tax or financial advice: these are 2026 federal estimates for a single filer taking the standard deduction, using the same method as the site's other guides. Your employer's payroll calendar, pay frequency, and benefit deductions change the per-check figures, and the right raise to ask for depends on your whole situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about a 5% raise and what it is really worth:

How much is a 5% raise on $60,000?

A 5% raise on a $60,000 salary is $3,000 a year, taking the salary to $63,000 before taxes. After 2026 federal income tax and FICA, you keep $2,410.50 of it — $360 goes to federal tax at the 12% marginal rate and $229.50 to Social Security and Medicare. That is $92.71 more per biweekly paycheck, or $200.88 more a month. The whole raise sits inside the 12% bracket, because taxable income moves from $43,900 to $46,900, both below the $50,400 line where the 22% bracket starts.

How much is a 5% raise per paycheck?

On a $60,000 salary paid biweekly, a 5% raise is $115.38 gross per paycheck and $92.71 after federal income tax and FICA. Paid weekly it is $57.69 gross and $46.36 kept; paid semi-monthly it is $125.00 gross and $100.44 kept per check. If you also contribute 6% to a traditional 401(k), the contribution takes another $6.92 per check from the raise, leaving $85.79 — the raise is still worth having, it just shares a slice with your retirement account.

Is a 5% raise good?

Yes — 5% is at the top of the typical merit-raise range of 3% to 5%, so it is a strong merit increase, not a token one. It also beats the benchmarks that decide whether a raise is real: the 2026 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment is 2.8%, and at 3% inflation a 5% raise is a 1.94% real raise, worth $1,165.05 of extra purchasing power on a $60,000 salary. A raise below 2.8% is a real pay cut against the cost of living, and a promotion raise is usually larger still, 10% to 20%.

How do you calculate a 5% raise?

Multiply your current pay by 1.05. On $60,000 that is $60,000 × 1.05 = $63,000, and the raise itself is $60,000 × 0.05 = $3,000. To work out a percentage from two salaries, divide the increase by the old salary, never the new one: ($63,000 − $60,000) ÷ $60,000 = 5%. Dividing by the new salary instead gives $3,000 ÷ $63,000 = 4.76%, which is the most common raise-math mistake and the one that makes a real 5% raise look smaller than it is.

Does a 5% raise beat inflation?

At 3% inflation, yes: a 5% nominal raise is a 1.94% real raise, because $1.05 ÷ $1.03 − 1 = 1.94%. On a $60,000 salary the $63,000 new pay is worth $61,165.05 in today's dollars, a genuine $1,165.05 gain in purchasing power. At 5% inflation the same raise is exactly a wash — $1.05 ÷ $1.05 − 1 = 0% — and at 2.8% inflation, the 2026 cost-of-living pace, the real gain is 2.14%. The raise only improves your position when it clears the inflation rate, which is why the percentage alone never tells the whole story.

What is a 5% raise on $50,000?

A 5% raise on a $50,000 salary is $2,500 a year, taking the salary to $52,500 before taxes. After 2026 federal income tax and FICA you keep $2,008.75 of it — $300.00 to federal tax at the 12% marginal rate and $191.25 to FICA — which is $77.26 more per biweekly paycheck, or $167.40 more a month. The same 5% is worth more in dollars at higher salaries and less at lower ones: $2,000 gross on $40,000, $3,750 on $75,000, and $5,000 on $100,000, with the kept share falling from about 80 cents to about 70 cents per dollar once the 22% bracket starts.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • A 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 gross and $2,410.50 kept — $360.00 to federal tax at the 12% marginal rate, $229.50 to FICA — which is $92.71 more per biweekly paycheck, $200.88 more a month, and about 80 cents of each extra dollar.
  • The kept share falls with your bracket — about 80 cents per dollar at 12%, about 70 cents at 22% — and the same 5% is $2,000 gross on $40,000, $2,500 on $50,000, $3,750 on $75,000, and $5,000 on $100,000.
  • A raise can never push your take-home pay down — only the $175.00 above the $50,400 line pays 22% on the $63,500 crossing example, so the federal tax on that $3,175.00 raise is $398.50, not $698.50, and the myth costs $300.00 in bad math.
  • 5% is a real raise in 2026 — a 1.94% real gain at 3% inflation, worth $1,165.05 of purchasing power on $60,000 — because it clears both the 2.8% cost-of-living pace and the 3.4% average wage growth.
  • A raise repeats and a bonus does not — five years of 5% raises are worth $48,114.78 of extra gross pay against a flat salary, while a $3,000 one-time bonus is worth $3,000, a $45,114.78 gap, even though year one is an exact tie at $2,410.50 kept.
  • Asking for 7% instead of 5% is worth $964.20 a year kept on a $60,000 salary — $37.08 per biweekly check — and $6,630.76 of extra gross pay over five years, because the gap compounds too.
  • A mid-year raise is worth half its headline in year one — a July 1 start pays $1,500.00 gross and $1,205.25 kept in the first year — and moving the effective date three months earlier is worth $602.63 kept.
  • Price your own raise before the conversation — run your salary and your percentage through the salary increase calculator, apply the 80-cent kept-share rule at the 12% rate, and walk in knowing the dollar value of the number you are asking for.

Sources & Method

Tax figures: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 — 2026 standard deduction $16,100 (single), brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, 24% to $201,775 of taxable income; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), per IRS Topic No. 424; withholding follows the IRS Publication 15-T percentage method. Benchmarks: Social Security cost-of-living adjustment 2.8% for 2026; Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Cost Index, private-sector wages and salaries up 3.4% over the 12 months ending March 2026; the 3% inflation rate in the real-raise table is a stated assumption, not a forecast. Cross-checks: the $60,000 take-home of $50,390.00 matches the site's $60,000-after-taxes guide; the $100,000 row's kept $3,517.50 matches the site's $100,000-after-taxes guide's $5,000-raise line; the $20-to-$21 hourly kept figure of $1,671.28 is exactly the site's $21-an-hour guide minus its $20-an-hour guide ($37,276.88 − $35,605.60); the 10-year compounding figure of $97,733.68 matches calculatorpark.com's independently computed table; the 6% 401(k) variant of $2,230.50 kept, $85.79 per biweekly check, matches calculatorzilo.com's independently computed figure. Competitor note: calculatorzilo.com (top result) has the strongest worked example — $60,000 at 5%, $2,231 kept with a 6% 401(k), a real-raise test at 3% inflation, and the 2026 brackets listed — but covers one salary only, applies FICA as a flat 7.65% simplification, and gives no ladder, no hourly version, no bracket-crossing example, and no compounding; michaelryanmoney.com gives gross figures only ($3,000, $115.38 a check) with no bracket-step tax math; calculatorpark.com has gross tables, an inflation table, and a 10-year compounding table but no take-home figures at all; payraisekit.com, salarycalchub.com, and onlycalculators.com are gross-only formula-and-table pages; thecalculatorsites.com adds the BLS 3.4% wage-growth and 2.8% COLA context but no take-home math. This article is general information, not tax or financial advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. A 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 gross and $2,410.50 kept — $360.00 to federal tax, $229.50 to FICA — which is $92.71 more per biweekly paycheck and about 80 cents of each extra dollar in your bank account.
  2. Only the slice of a raise above a bracket line pays the higher rate: on a $63,500-to-$66,675 raise that crosses into the 22% bracket, just $175.00 is taxed at 22%, so the federal tax is $398.50 — not $698.50 — and a raise can never lower your take-home pay.
  3. A raise repeats and a bonus does not: five years of 5% raises are worth $48,114.78 of extra gross pay against a flat salary, while a $3,000 one-time bonus is worth $3,000 — and asking for 7% instead of 5% is worth $964.20 a year kept, $6,630.76 over five years.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 6, 2026.
